item.title: Lecture: Can a Fading Language Come Back?
item.summary: A linguistics lecture on what makes a language endangered and what successful revival efforts, such as those for Hebrew and Welsh, tend to have in common.
item.transcript_text: Good afternoon, everyone. Last week we discussed why languages become endangered, so today I want to turn to the more hopeful question: can a language that's fading be brought back? The short answer is yes, sometimes, but it's never easy, and it never happens by accident. Let's start with a distinction. A language is generally considered endangered when children stop learning it at home, even if many adults still speak it. Once that chain between generations breaks, the number of speakers tends to fall steadily, because each generation of speakers is smaller than the last. Revival, then, is essentially about repairing that chain. The most frequently cited example is Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly in religious and written contexts, and then became an everyday spoken language again, with children growing up speaking it as their first language. Welsh is a rather different kind of case. It never stopped being spoken, but it was under considerable pressure, and its position has been strengthened through schools, broadcasting and its use in public life. So what do successful efforts tend to have in common? Broadly speaking, three things. First, education, and particularly immersion schooling, where children learn other subjects through the language. Second, visibility: the language appears on signs, on television and, increasingly, online. And third, and perhaps most importantly, prestige. If young people associate a language only with the past, or with their grandparents' village, they're unlikely to choose it. If they see it as useful and, frankly, a bit cool, the picture changes. Next week, we'll look at the role of technology in all of this, from keyboards to voice assistants.
